description: A friendly research group that contains six people who are united in the idea of creating a project that solves a possible problem that would happen in a space mission.
summary: We have developed a health monitoring program for a possible Mars mission, and to test the program, we have created a simulation that scaled a Mars mission to 60 days. The astronaut travels like on the ISS for the first 15 days, stays on Mars for 30 days and returns in the last 15 days. Every day, the program checks nine signals, including sleep, body temperature, blood oxygen, water intake, exercise, morale and a short focus test. Each value is compared with limits made for the ISS or for Mars, and it is marked as Normal, Caution or Critical. Because messages between Earth and Mars can take up to 24 minutes, the program gives advice directly to the astronaut first. It only sends a message to Earth when the problem is serious. Our limits are based on NASA data, and we made our own estimates for Mars.
details:
The Problem

During a Mars mission, astronauts cannot rely on medical support from Earth. A message takes a long time to travel between Mars and Earth, and returning home quickly is not possible. Long missions also bring health risks such as bone and muscle loss, poor sleep, and stress, so astronauts need to notice problems and act on their own.

Our research

Research started with the changes in an astronaut’s body and daily life during a long mission, and which of these changes the astronaut can notice and act on. And these were:

  • Space physiology: the effect of weightlessness and partial gravity on body temperature, bone, muscle, sleep, and fluid balance
  • Environments: We compared Earth, the ISS, and Mars (gravity, habitat air pressure, length of day, distance from Earth), because the same value can be normal in one place and a warning sign in another.
  • Current systems: We found that these systems mostly depend on doctors on Earth, and astronauts giving the information to the Earth by themselves.
  • Habits and mental health: We researched astronauts’ sleep, exercise, focus, and morale.

Our Own Theories

No human has lived on Mars, so for many values, there is no measured data. In these cases, we built our own estimates from physics and from what is known about the ISS, and we mark them as estimates in our code.

  • Limits: We chose wide limits for values that are often low in ISS and Mars, like sleep, morale, exercise time, sleep hours and body temperature so the system does not warn astronauts too often. Too many warnings make people stop paying attention (alarm fatigue).

    ISS and Mars compared
    Gravity felt: ISS: Weightless / Mars: 38% of Earth
    Core body temperature: ISS: ~38.0 °C (Stahn, 2017) / Mars: ~37.3 °C (our estimate)
    Sleep per night: ISS: ~6 hours (Barger, 2014) / Mars: ~6 hours 15 minutes (our estimate)
    Daily exercise: ISS: ~2 hours (NASA) / Mars: ~105 minutes, none on surface walk days (our estimate)
    Water intake: ISS: 3.0–4.5 liters (our estimate) / Mars: 3.5–5.0 liters (our estimate)
    Blood oxygen: ISS: 95–100% (cabin air like sea level) / Mars: 93–100% (our estimate)
    Resting heart rate: ISS: 60–100 beats/min / Mars: 60–100 beats/min (Earth values)
    Breathing rate: ISS: 12–20 breaths/min / Mars: 12–20 breaths/min (Earth values)
    Morale (1–5): ISS: 3–5, by mission phase (our estimate) / Mars: 2–5, lowest during long research (our estimate)
    Message delay to Earth: ISS: A few seconds / Mars: Up to 24 minutes

Our project’s basic function

  • It checks the astronaut’s health data every day and compares it to limits for each environment.
  • If it finds a problem, it sends a message to the astronaut and to Earth only when necessary.
  • It tracks resting heart rate, blood oxygen, sleep, breathing rate, core body temperature, exercise, water intake, a daily 30-second focus test, and morale.

Note: In this prototype, we simulate the data. In a real mission, it would come from wearable sensors and the station’s existing systems.

How our project works

  • It simulates a 60-day mission scaled from a possible Mars mission: 15 days of travel, 30 days on Mars, and 15 days back, with different situations an astronaut might go through.
  • Each value is marked Normal, Caution, or Critical using environment-specific limits.
